Small Theft Ring. Outcasts find each other eventually. Gain Stealth or Sleight of Hand.
Wild Companion. Beast or half-broken soul kept near your camp for a while. Gain Animal Handling or Insight.
Rotten Bargain. You traded clean conscience for one more month alive. Gain Manipulation or Survival.
Silent Country. You learned the shape of land folk fear after dark. Gain Scouting or Lore. Gain one rumor.
Useful Monster. Folk who hated your face still used your hands. Gain Manipulation or Melee. This may be your Pride.
Bandit Camp. You drifted among worse company and learned from it. Gain Stealth or Scouting.
Settlement Edge. You survived by moving just close enough to the walls. Gain Insight or Move.
Night Deal. Something traded in whispers became your business for a season. Gain Manipulation or Sleight of Hand.
Ambush or Escape. You learned when to strike and when to vanish. Gain Melee or Stealth.
Cold Wisdom. Hard years taught you to read men faster than weather. Gain Insight or Survival.

segments.text: Outcast Fourth Turn: Return, Revenge, or Vanishing

rows: No Way Back. The door truly shut behind you. Gain Survival or Endurance. You must change path next cycle or remain Outcast under narrowing tax.
Taken in by the Damned. A gang, hidden camp, or harsh patron gave you belonging of a sort. Gain Manipulation or Stealth.
Revenge Taken. You hurt one of those who cast you out. Gain Melee or Insight. Gain one enemy and one grim satisfaction. This may be your Dark Secret.
Return in Secret. You stepped back into old ground under another name or by moonlight. Gain Move or Manipulation.
Worse than Alone. Someone beside you proved more dangerous than solitude. Gain Insight or Scouting.
Endured Anyway. Survival itself became a kind of strength. Gain Endurance or Insight. You may take one Outcast advancement benefit even if the later roll fails. This may be your Pride.
Beaten, branded, or stoned out of a place. Gain one scar.
Betrayed by one of the few you trusted. Gain one rival.
Starved, froze, or nearly drowned before crawling back. Gain one fear or chronic pain.
Branded a thief, plague-bearer, or witch. Lower Standing by 1 in one settlement.
You hurt someone who did not deserve it. Gain one dark secret.
The road outside society has changed you too much. Your next cycle must change path or gain one extra Wear before it begins.

Found, judged, and driven out a second time, further and harder. Gain two scars, lower Standing by 1 in two settlements, and gain one fear tied to community, firelight, or being known. Your next cycle must change path or begins with two Wear.
One hidden-camp, outlaw, or edge-of-settlement contact
Hidden camp gear, knife, blanket, and practical survival kit
One rumor about a forgotten path, outlaw hoard, or place decent folk avoid
Knife, blanket, patched gear, and camp kit
One hidden contact and one settlement that wants you gone
D6 silver in stolen or buried form
One scar and one story that cannot be told in every firelight
One hidden shelter, outlaw trail, or buried cache
One rumor about a ruin, outlaw band, or enemy worth hunting

segments.html: After the last cycle, roll on the mustering-out table for your final path. The number of rolls equals the turns you completed in that path, to a maximum of 3. Choose one result and discard the others.

This gives you the practical remains of the life you just left behind — gear, silver, a contact, a rival, a rumor, or a scar that still matters. A longer commitment earns more options; a short or desperate stint earns one chance at whatever it left you.

If a mustering-out result duplicates something you already hold, keep both if the story allows it or replace one with a related alternative. Two daggers from two different lives tell different stories.
The life generator may leave you with nothing but scars and stories. After mustering out, check what the dice gave you against the minimum starting gear for your chosen profession:

• Every character starts with a waterskin and a travel backpack regardless of rolls.
  • If the generator did not provide a weapon, take the cheapest weapon listed in your profession's starting gear.
  • If your profession's standard starting gear includes armor (Champion and Fighter: studded leather), and the generator did not provide any, take that armor.
  • If you are a Champion, take a closed helmet if the generator did not provide one, and a small shield if the generator did not provide one.
  • If your profession's standard starting gear includes a mount (Rider) or instrument (Minstrel), and the generator did not provide one, you start with that item. The road left you with at least this much.
  • If the generator did not grant you any coins at all, roll your profession's starting coin dice once. This is the last money from the last job.
itemLiHtmls: • Every character starts with a waterskin and a travel backpack regardless of rolls.
• If the generator did not provide a weapon, take the cheapest weapon listed in your profession's starting gear.
• If your profession's standard starting gear includes armor (Champion and Fighter: studded leather), and the generator did not provide any, take that armor.
• If you are a Champion, take a closed helmet if the generator did not provide one, and a small shield if the generator did not provide one.

• If your profession's standard starting gear includes a mount (Rider) or instrument (Minstrel), and the generator did not provide one, you start with that item. The road left you with at least this much.
• If the generator did not grant you any coins at all, roll your profession's starting coin dice once. This is the last money from the last job.

segments.html: Keep everything the dice gave you on top of the floor. The gear floor exists to prevent a character from walking into session one unarmed and broke — it does not replace the generator's results.

Gear granted by events and mustering-out should be interpreted as specific items during play. "A serviceable weapon" means a real weapon from the gear chapter — the player and GM agree on what fits the story. When in doubt, pick the simplest version.

After mustering out, look back at the life the dice built. Every character carries something forward — a debt unsettled, an enemy unmet, a rumor that still pulls, a scar whose source was never repaid. Something from that road is not over yet.
Choose one piece of unfinished business from your life's accumulated fiction. Frame it as a question your character cannot yet answer:

• Where did the ferry captain go after I could not repay him?
  • Who gave the order that broke my company?
  • What sleeps beneath the shrine they burned?
itemLiHtmls: • Where did the ferry captain go after I could not repay him?
• Who gave the order that broke my company?
• What sleeps beneath the shrine they burned?

segments.html: There are two kinds:

rows: A debt to pay, a face to find, a place to revisit. Can be settled in one to three sessions.
A sworn oath, a wrong that shaped you, a truth the world owes you. May take the whole campaign.

segments.html: Wear determines the weight. A character who stumbled through the life generator with few
failures carries less behind them. A character beaten, broken, captured, and exiled carries debts the road will not forgive.

rows: Choose either a Short Errand or a Life Quest.
Choose a Life Quest. The past left too much undone for a quick answer.
Choose a Life Quest. The GM also names one Short Errand drawn from your hardest Wear source — the scar, feud, or debt that weighs heaviest.

segments.html: The question does not need to name the answer. It needs to point the character toward play.

Resolving Unfinished Business. A Short Errand is resolved when the character confronts the source and acts — pays the debt, finds the face, visits the place, settles the score. A Life Quest is resolved when the central question is answered, not necessarily when the character gets what they wanted. The GM decides when a piece of unfinished business is done and awards the XP at that moment.
If a character dies before resolving a Life Quest, the question passes to the next character the player creates in the same campaign. The old road has weight, and someone always inherits it.
The life path does not replace the professions in Chapter 2. It leads into them.
Use these rules:
• If your last cycle used a profession path, that path is your default profession.
itemLiHtmls: • If your last cycle used a profession path, that path is your default profession.

segments.html:
• If your last cycle used a crisis path, choose between the profession paths from your two previous cycles.
  • If you completed only one profession path across your whole history, you must use that profession.
  • If no profession path was ever completed, choose the profession tied to the skill family in which you hold the most ranks.
itemLiHtmls: • If your last cycle used a crisis path, choose between the profession paths from your two previous cycles.
• If you completed only one profession path across your whole history, you must use that profession.
• If no profession path was ever completed, choose the profession tied to the skill family in which you hold the most ranks.

segments.html: Champion and Fighter draw on much of the same skill family, but Champion is not a fallback profession. You may choose Champion only if you completed a Champion path. When these rules otherwise leave the choice between them, choose Fighter.
Once your profession is set, continue with the profession rules in Chapter 2:

• Choose your profession talent. Mark 1 tally toward your chosen profession talent. This is your profession talent seed — the life you lived before play earns you that first mark. If advancement benefits already granted marks in the same talent, add the seed mark to that total. Talent marks from the life generator convert to ranks using the same progression table as skills. If sustained focus pushed a talent to Rank 3, keep it — the narrowing taxes and lost breadth already paid for that concentration.
  • A Champion who chooses Path of the Holy Vow should build its Vow or Oath from the named oath, cause, charge, or patron established during the life generator whenever possible.
  • Choose your general talents by age.

segments.html: Languages, Willpower, appearance, and name follow the rest of Chapter 2 without change.

The contacts, rivals, enemies, rumors, and scars accumulated during the life generator are not points to spend. They are the world's grip on your character. The GM should treat them as live threads — people who might appear, debts that might come due, places that might matter. The more fiction the generator built, the more the world already knows your name.

Jorrh

Jorrh is an Adult Alderlander human. Three completed cycles.

He

rolls Squire on the childhood foundation table — Melee 1 and Healing 1, Strength and Empathy favored. One former master still remembers his service. That master is the closest thing to a father he remembers.

First cycle: Fighter. The border needed swords more than prayers. The first and second turn is covered by childhood — shield-drills and cold camps along the Alderlander marches. For the third turn he passes the turn test and rolls a 1 on Fighter Third Turn: First Blood. He killed at arm's length and learned the sound it makes. Gain Melee. The fourth turn fails — he rolls a 2 on Fighter Mishaps: Left for dead. One scar across the collarbone. One enemy who thinks he should have stayed buried. He fails the advancement roll and must leave the Fighter path.

A wound like that changes a life. He was carried out of the ditch by strangers and set down at a crossroads with nothing but a bad shoulder and a name he could not use at home. The next cycle writes itself.

Second cycle: Drifter. He does not choose this — the dice choose it for him through the forced-life table. Four turns of rootless walking. He gains Survival from sleeping rough, Insight from watching strangers' faces for threat or pity, Scouting

from finding the old Mist-year shelters, and Manipulation from learning to beg without quite calling it begging. One hidden shelter from the Blood Mist years is the closest thing he has to property. The road also leaves him with a debt to a ferryman who fed him through a bad week and one village that made it clear he was not welcome back.

At the end of that cycle the dice decide again. He passes the Drifter advancement roll but chooses to leave the path anyway. He has enough Melee and enough anger to try fighting again.

Third cycle: Fighter. Second run means the narrowing tax applies — turn tests at -1, mishaps at +1. This time the turns land better. He picks up Endurance and more Melee, earns a serviceable weapon, and gains one scar with a story behind it. The advancement roll succeeds.

Results. Jorrh ends with 12 marks (2 from childhood, 10 from resolved turns). His marks cluster in Melee (4 marks — Rank 3), Survival (3 marks — Rank 3), Scouting (2 marks — Rank 2), Insight (2 marks — Rank 2), and Healing (1 mark — Rank 1). That is the shape of someone who fought, lost, walked hungry, and fought again. He has two scars, one enemy, one debt, one hidden shelter, and one old master who still believes in him.

When he rolled

First Blood in his first cycle, the event carried a tag: This may be your Pride. He notes it as the place his Pride comes from. That note matters to the story, not to the rule. His Dark Secret comes from the Fighter profession entry.

His Wear is 1 — only one pair of consecutive failures across three cycles. At 0–1 Wear he may choose either a Short Errand or a Life Quest for his unfinished business. He chooses a Life Quest. The man who left him in that ditch is still out there. His question: Who buried me, and do they still walk free? That is worth 25 XP when the answer comes.

He does not feel a made-up hero. He feels like a man who got knocked down twice and kept standing up, not because the world rewarded it but because he did not know how to do anything else.

His profession is Fighter. He marks 1 tally toward Defender as his profession talent seed. The rest of the chapter takes him from here. Torvin is an Old Dwarf. Four completed cycles.

He rolls Smith's Apprentice — Crafting 1 and Melee 1, Strength and Wits favored. He still owes loyalty to a forge and a dead master's memory.

First cycle: Laborer. The forge burned. The master died in the fire. There was no trade to inherit and no guild to claim him. Torvin spent four years

carrying stone and timber for a dwarven quarry crew — the kind of work that pays in bread and bruises and nothing else. He gains Might, Crafting, Endurance, and Insight. The work leaves him with one employer contact (a quarry boss who respected his silence) and a scar across three fingers where a stone-saw bit.

Second cycle: Peddler. The quarry boss put him on a supply run and never called him back. Torvin discovered he could price goods by weight and smell and that his hands, ugly as they were, could mend things other traders threw away. He gains Manipulation, Crafting, Insight, and Scouting. He also gains a trade contact at a mountain fair and a rival — another peddler who accused him of undercutting prices on repaired ironwork.

Third cycle: Peddler (continued, narrowing tax applies). Torvin stays in trade. Turn tests at -1 now. The risk of mishaps climbs. He gains more Manipulation and Insight, learns a profitable route through the crags of Far Vivend, and rolls a 6 on Third Turn — Map in the Margins. A torn page in a dead man's ledger points to something buried beneath a ruin near Beldersand. He gains one rumor the GM will use later.

Fourth cycle: Captive. The Forced-Life Table sends him here — result 1, war

captivity. Raiders from the Harga Wastes took his wagon, his goods, and two years of his life. He gains Endurance, Insight, Survival, and Stealth. He also gains one fellow survivor as a contact, one captor as an enemy, and one hidden route through a stronghold cellar that he will never forget.

Results. Torvin ends with 16 marks. His marks lean into Crafting (4 marks — Rank 3), Insight (4 marks — Rank 3), Manipulation (3 marks — Rank 3), Endurance (2 marks — Rank 2), Survival (1 mark — Rank 1), Melee (1 mark — Rank 1), and Stealth (1 mark — Rank 1). A trader shaped by stone, road, and chain. He has two contacts, two scars, one rival, one enemy, one rumor, and one escape route. He is old, slow, and knows what things cost — all things, not just the ones with prices.

No tagged event offered a Pride or Dark Secret during his generation. He takes both from the Peddler profession entry.

His Wear is 2 — two runs of consecutive failures across four cycles, one in the narrowing third cycle and one during captivity. At 2–3 Wear he chooses one lingering fear from the Wear tier. His unfinished business is a Life Quest — the past left too much undone for a quick answer. His question: What became of the raider captain from the Harga Wastes who kept me in

chains, and does he still trade in lives? That is worth 25 XP when answered.

His profession is Peddler. He marks 1 tally toward Sharp Tongue as his profession talent seed. The scars and the ledger tell the same story.

Use this table after every character has finished the life generator. The stronger backstories make the table better, not weaker — a prison escape, shared debt, or bloody battle carries more weight when every adventurer already comes in with old roads behind them.
Roll D66 or choose.

rows: Caravan. You participated in a caravan that traveled through the Forbidden Lands. Maybe you were employed as a guard, maybe you were a guide. During the journey you got to know some adventurers who were part of the caravan. After many hardships you finally reached your destination, and in the process, you found new friends.

Ambush. During a journey through the Forbidden Lands you and your party were ambushed. Your friends were slain in the battle, but you were rescued at the last minute by some strangers who brought you to safety. You have been friends ever since.

Imprisoned. You were captured and thrown in a dungeon. It may have been robbers, soldiers, or Rust Brothers that imprisoned you. But you were not alone. In the dungeon, there were other adventurers in the same situation. Together, you managed to escape.

All Night Bender. You do not remember much of the evening, only that there was a proper celebration. In the haze, you met some drinking buddies in the form of other adventurers, and you shared tankards of wine, stories, and even had a little bit of a tussle before dawn broke. You have been friends since.

Searched for an Artifact. You searched long and hard for the treasure, traveled across the land, and braved dangers. But just when you were about to get your hands on the artifact, it turned out that some other adventurers had the same plan. It was a precarious dilemma, but on the way to the nearest village to appraise the treasure, you realized that you had more in common than you had imagined. You split the money and became friends.

Saved by Adventurers. You were in trouble. Maybe you had been captured by the Iron Guard, maybe you had been caught by slave traders. But fate had other plans, and you were dramatically saved by some other adventurers at the last moment.

Captured by Another Adventurer. At one time you were enemies. You were outwitted and captured by some other adventurers. But during your captivity, your animosity turned to friendship. You realized that you had even more dangerous enemies in common and joined forces.

Childhood Friends. You grew up together with another adventurer. You played together, shared meals, and met each other's families. But something happened one day that caused you to go your separate ways. Many years passed until the day your paths crossed once more. You are not the same people you were when you were kids, but you share a strong bond.

Mutual Debt. You do not really know how it happened, but suddenly you found yourself owing an absurd amount of silver to a person you really do not want to put yourself at odds with. But you were not alone. Another group of adventurers had put themselves in the same situation, and together you managed to amass enough silver to pay off the debt.

Fought a Bloody Battle. You fought in a battle where many lives were lost. It was a difficult fight. Maybe you came close to dying yourself, but in the end, you found brothers and sisters in arms in the form of some other adventurers. Together, you made it through the bloody day with your lives intact. But the scars remain.

Hunted by Rust Brothers. Something you did was perceived as an insult against Rust or Heme. The Rust Brothers did not take your action kindly, and sent the Iron Guard to capture you. In your flight, you found a group of other adventurers in the same plight. Together you outsmarted your pursuers. Maybe they will catch your scent again.

Plundered the Same Dungeon. You searched long and hard for the treasure, braved the dangers of the dungeon, and finally found it, only to realize that you were not alone. Other adventurers had followed the same map, looking for the same treasure. A delicate dilemma, but somehow you became friends despite it all.

Caught in a Storm. One dark night, you sought shelter from a terrible storm. In the sheltering crevice you found a few other adventurers warming themselves by a fire. You endured the storm together, and during the long night, told each other legends of ancient heroes and monsters. You have been friends since.

Caught by Slavers. You were caught by a brutal gang of slave traders. Beaten within an inch of your life and caged like a dog. In the cages, you met some other unfortunate adventurers who had suffered the same fate. Somehow you managed to escape the slavers. Maybe you exacted your revenge then, maybe you still thirst for it.

Captured by Saurians. You wandered too far into the marshes. Suddenly, you were lost in the fog with only the sounds of strange creatures for company. In that moment, you were surrounded by dozens of Saurians, hissing amongst themselves. You were brought to their village deep in the wetlands, and met a few other adventurers who had been captured the same way. You eventually managed to escape. Maybe you hate Saurians now, maybe you acquired unexpected allies.

Hired Guards. You and the other adventurers were hired to guard someone. Maybe it was a trade caravan, maybe the traveling child of a lord. During the mission, you overcame dangers and realized that you worked well together.

Trial by Combat. Somehow you got into a fight with another adventurer. After having exchanged insults, curses, and threats, you agreed to settle your conflict through trial by combat. Both of you fought bravely and both were wounded, but in the end, you had to give up the fight when you ran out of steam. After the duel, it was as if your animosity had dissolved. Instead, you became friends, and since that day you are inseparable.

Survived a Shipwreck. You traveled on a ship that happened upon dire straits. The ship was smashed to bits against sharp rocks in the storm, and most of the crew perished in the waves. But you and some other adventurers miraculously managed to survive. It took days before you were found, but you made it. Since that day you share an unforgettable memory.

segments.html: "A silver coin becomes ten in the hands of a patient merchant. A fool with ten lets them slip away." — Bartel the Ledger, factor to the Gristle's company

The Forbidden Lands economy rests on more than coin and contract. It rests on movement — goods crossing the roads, boats moving down the rivers, traders following the seasons from settlement to settlement. A fellowship with silver and audacity can join that flow, assembling a caravan and running profit along established routes or cutting new paths through unmapped country.

A caravan is any organized trade expedition that moves goods between settlements for profit. It may be as small as a peddler with a laden mule, or as large as a six-wagon train with guards, factors, and a scout riding ahead. The rules scale. All caravans share three components: the transport that carries the cargo, the cargo itself, and the people who make it work.

Caravan capacity is measured in load units. One load unit equals approximately 10 Normal-weight items (100 units of weight using the carrying system described in Chapter 2). Animals and vehicles have load capacities:

rows: Reliable, cheap. Navigates terrain where wagons cannot pass.
Faster empty, same speed burdened with cargo.
Cheap, stubborn, eats less than a mule.
Strong and cheap. Cannot cross marsh, mountain, or dense forest.
Standard trade wagon. Loses speed on unimproved trails.
Fast downstream (+1 hex/day) / Slow upstream (−1 hex/day)
High capacity but route-locked. Requires PIER to load and unload.
Maximum capacity on land. Cannot leave maintained roads.

segments.html: Terrain and speed. Road-dependent transport (wagons, heavy wagons) travels at listed speed on maintained roads and at half speed on trails. Off-road, wagons cannot move at all without spending a full quarter day per hex to clear a path. Mules and horses handle all terrain at listed speed. River barges are locked to their waterways but move quickly downstream.

Animal upkeep. Each draft or pack animal consumes 1 unit of FOOD per day (6 copper worth of grain or forage; free in grassland or forest if the caravan spends a quarter day grazing). WATER must be carried or found at rivers and streams. Vehicles require occasional repair — treat as a CRAFTING check using Carpentry or Smithing,
difficulty 1, after every 10 days of road travel or after any damage event.
A caravan requires people to function — not every role must be filled, but a caravan that lacks necessary people will struggle:

rows: Leads the expedition, decides routes, handles trade and sales
Usually a PC. If hired as an NPC, 2 silver/day.
Handles animals, loads and unloads cargo, maintains gear
One per two wagons or four pack animals.
Chapter 12's mercenary pay rates apply to larger escort forces.
Manages trade at the destination, negotiates with buyers
Requires PATH OF THE CARAVAN Rank 3 or an NPC with MANIPULATION 3+.
Rides ahead, watches for hazards, finds campsites
Uses SCOUTING to provide advance warning of encounters.

segments.html: A bare caravan — one peddler with a pack mule — needs nobody but the owner. A standard four-wagon caravan needs one or two drovers and one or two guards. A large caravan of six or more wagons needs the full complement: factors, scouts, multiple drovers, and a proper guard force.

Wages and discipline. Employees are paid daily from the caravan's fund. An unpaid employee leaves after 1D6 days, taking what they can carry — supplies, goods, or a mule if they can ride. Wages come out of the operating budget before profit is calculated. A slow journey spends more on wages and leaves less room for profit.
Loading a caravan is a quarter-day activity. One character supervises the work and makes a CRAFTING roll (no talent required — this is pure logistics). Difficulty 0.

rows: Loaded but poorly secured. The first rough terrain hex or hazard event causes 1D6 silver of cargo damage — shifted loads, broken goods, spilled grain.
Adequately loaded. No bonus, no penalty.
Well loaded. The first cargo damage event of the journey is ignored — the lashing held.
Expertly loaded. As above, plus available load capacity increases by 10% (rounded up) due to efficient packing.

segments.html: Characters with PATH OF THE ARTISAN gain relevant bonuses. PATH OF THE CARAVAN R2+ characters roll for results even at the baseline and reduce the failure state to a -1 modifier instead of damage.
Cargo divides into seven categories. Each has a typical buy price range per load unit at origin, a margin of profit, and handling requirements:

rows: Low risk, low reward. Always in demand somewhere.
Moderate value. Demand varies by settlement.
High value. Fragile — breakage risk on rough roads.
Demand driven by settlements with specific stronghold functions.
Some settlements restrict trade. Requires PATH OF THE CARAVAN R4.
Extremely Rare. Available only in certain locations.
Walk themselves but need feed, water, and protection from predators.

segments.html: The following tables list the base prices for goods commonly carried by caravans. A load unit of bulk goods (grain, salt, ore, timber) holds approximately 10 Normal-weight items. Single high-value items (weapons, instruments, fine cloth) are packed together into mixed loads at the load-unit scale, or carried individually.

All prices are origin prices — what the caravan pays to buy the goods at the source settlement. The sell price at the destination is determined by the supply multiplier and seasonal multiplier described later in this chapter.

segments.text: Bulk Staples (5–15 silver per load unit)

rows: Staple food. Always in demand. Spoils if wet.
Preservative. High demand in settlements without a salt source.
Cheap protein. Available at river and coastal settlements.
Heavy, low value. Only profitable on short routes to treeless settlements.
Produced at settlements with sheepfolds. Needed by settlements with a tailor.
Milled grain. Higher value, slightly more perishable.
Animal feed. Seasonal demand spikes in winter.
Candle-making, waterproofing, soap. Rendered from slaughtered animals.

segments.text: Craft Goods (15–40 silver per load unit)

rows: Standard textile. Needed everywhere clothing wears out.
Demand at settlements with smiths, armorers, and saddlers.
Mixed tool loads. High demand at settlements without a forge.
Universal demand. Heavy for their value.
Fragile. Breakage risk on rough roads.
Higher margin than raw grain. Spoils in 1 week.
Iron fittings, brackets, barrel hoops. Small, dense, valuable.

segments.text: Luxury Goods (40–100 silver per load unit)

rows: Universal demand at inns. Fragile — breakage risk.
Extremely high value-to-weight. Demand at wealthy settlements.
Needed by settlements with cloth production.
Cannot be produced in the Forbidden Lands. Import only.
Temple and luxury demand. Light, high margin.

segments.text: Raw Materials (10–30 silver per load unit)

rows: Heavy. Only valuable to settlements with a forge.
The universal craft metal. High demand at any forge.
Heavy, cheap. Profitable only on short routes to treeless areas.
Extremely heavy. Only moved by ox cart on short routes.
Spoil within 1 week if not tanned. Demand at tanneries.
Medicinal and magical use. Potency fades after 5–10 days.
Needed for glassware, lenses, alchemical vessels.

segments.text: Arms and Armor (30–80 silver per load unit)

segments.html: Trading arms requires PATH OF THE CARAVAN R4 to use the talent network. Without it, a caravan can carry weapons physically but receives no talent bonuses. Some settlements restrict arms trade — the GM determines local law.

rows: Universal demand. Low margin but always sellable.
Work and war tools. High demand after conflict or frontier settlement.
Higher value. Demand varies by settlement militancy.
Cheap to make, always in demand for militia and defense.
Expensive, heavy. Demand at military settlements and wealthy strongholds.
Consumable. Always in demand at settlements with archers or hunters.

segments.text: Specialty Goods (50–200 silver per load unit)

rows: High demand at settlements without a healer.
Demand at temples, sorcerer towers, and apothecaries.
Extremely high value. Demand at temples and learned courts.
Restricted. Confiscated if found during customs inspection.
Temple demand. Some settlements ban rival faiths.
Unique items. Price determined by buyer, not market.
Demand among explorers, captains, and caravan masters.
Low value. Sold to settlements restocking after winter losses.
Wool and meat. Demand at settlements with empty pastures.
Cheap meat source. Commonly moved in small herds.
Milk and meat. High value. Vulnerable to predators on the road.
Draft animal. Demand at settlements needing transport.
High demand at settlements without a horse breeder.
Premium price at settlements needing mounts.
Military demand only. Extreme profit if the buyer exists.
Demand at isolated settlements and caravans.

segments.html: Some cargo spoils. Dried grain lasts indefinitely if kept dry. Fresh fish spoils in two or three days. Wine survives anything short of breakage. Herbs lose potency after a week in heat.
Track perishability only for time-sensitive goods. As a general rule:

rows: Spoilage — total loss if unsold in time
Potency loss — sell price halves after shelf life

segments.html: Luxury goods and glassware are fragile. When a caravan crosses rough terrain (marsh, mountain, dense forest) or suffers a hazard event, fragile cargo must pass a breakage check: roll 1D6 per load unit of fragile cargo. On a 1, that load unit takes 25% damage (round up in silver value). On a 1–2 if the terrain is mountain.
A loading roll that achieved 2+ ⚔️ negates the first breakage check of the journey. PATH OF THE CARAVAN R4 allows the caravan master to
designate one load unit of fragile cargo as personally secured, exempting it from all breakage checks.

Trade profit comes from arbitrage: buy where goods are cheap and sell where they are expensive. The supply system uses four tiers — Common, Uncommon, Rare, and Extremely Rare — to describe how available a good is at a given settlement. A Common item is cheap to buy there. A Rare item commands a premium. The same good can sit at different supply tiers in different settlements depending on geography, stronghold functions, and season.
The fundamental rule:
Buy at origin price. Sell at destination price. The difference is your margin — minus travel costs, wages, hazards, and tolls.
Each settlement has a trade profile — what it produces cheaply and what it needs at a premium. The GM assigns or generates these based on the
settlement's geography, size, and stronghold functions:

rows: Iron tools, weapons, salt, cloth, luxury goods
Grain, iron, salt, weapons, craft goods
Food, cloth, timber, medicine, luxury goods
Fish, rope, river trade goods, barge access
Food, luxury goods, craft goods, raw materials

segments.html: Price multipliers by supply level:

These multipliers apply to the buy price at origin. The GM adjusts for local conditions — a famine settlement might pay ×3.0 for grain even if grain is normally Common. Seasonal scarcity (described below) applies to trade goods as much as to work contracts.
When a character uses ASK AROUND at a settlement with a MARKETPLACE or among caravan folk, trade rumors are available as a reward for success. A successful roll reveals one or more of:

• Demand rumor: "Ironmere is desperate for salt — their mine ran dry last season." Indicates Rare supply at a specific settlement.
  • Supply rumor: "The elves at Green Dale are selling pelts cheap — too many, too few buyers." Indicates Common supply at origin.
  • Hazard rumor: "Bandits took a wagon on the Stillmire road last tenday." Indicates a specific route is dangerous.
  • Price rumor: "Spices out of the Amber Crossing are double the normal rate since the pass closed." Price spike at a location.

• Supply rumor: "The elves at Green Dale are selling pelts cheap — too many, too few buyers." Indicates Common supply at origin.

segments.html: • Competition rumor: "Three caravans already left for Hollowford this week." Destination market may be saturated.
itemLiHtmls: • Competition rumor: "Three caravans already left for Hollowford this week." Destination market may be saturated.

segments.html: Trade rumors travel along caravan routes at the speed described in Chapter 8 (10+ hexes per season on well-traveled roads). They age — only as current as the last trader who passed through.
Before departure, the caravan master chooses a route. This is a planning decision, not a roll. The players study the map and decide. Key route factors:

rows: More hexes = more days = more wages, feed, and hazard exposure.
Road: full speed. Trail: half speed for wagons (pack animals unaffected). Off-road: pack animals only.
Winter: +50% travel time, doubled feed costs, increased hazard frequency. Spring thaw: rivers flood, fords close, barges run fast.
Bandit lairs, monster territories, toll stations, hostile settlements.
Settlements with TOLL HOUSE charge 1–3 silver per wagon or 1 silver per load unit. Safe passage through hostile territory costs more.
Rivers provide water. Grassland provides grazing. Deserts and mountains require carried supplies.
A stronghold-built ROAD reduces travel time by one quarter day per two hexes. A BRIDGE eliminates river-crossing delays and risks.

segments.html: A caravan moves at the speed of its slowest transport. A wagon caravan on a road moves two hexes per day (one hex per hiking quarter day). Pack mule caravans move slightly faster on good terrain but cannot exceed three hexes per day.

Scout procedure. A caravan with a scout can detect hazards one hex ahead. The scout spends a quarter day riding forward and uses SCOUTING against the terrain's base difficulty (Chapter 8). Scout success grants reaction time to hazards — ambushes can be seen, routes can be changed, bandits can be tracked.

Camp. Caravans follow the standard Make Camp procedure. Large caravans (4+ wagons) require extra setup — one quarter day instead of one action. The camp is larger, louder, and easier to spot. Random encounter checks gain +1 to the hazard die while the caravan camps.

March order. Before each day's travel, the caravan master sets march order: scouts forward, cargo in the middle, guards distributed. March order matters when ambush or terrain events occur — it determines who is exposed first.

A caravan with a river barge (or a hired barge at 5 silver/day) can move along navigable rivers. Downstream travel gains +1 hex/day. Upstream travel suffers −1 hex/day. River travel avoids most land-based hazards (no bandits, no difficult terrain, no road tolls) but introduces its own: rapids, river pirates, grounding in shallows, and portage at waterfalls.
Loading barges requires a PIER at both origin and destination, or a half day of improvised loading at a riverbank (with breakage risk: roll 1D6 per load unit; cargo damage on a 1).
When the caravan arrives at its destination, the caravan master sells the cargo. This is not automatic. It is a procedure that takes time and negotiation.

Selling cargo is a quarter-day activity. The caravan master (or a factor acting on their behalf) makes a MANIPULATION roll to represent the process: finding buyers, negotiating terms, displaying quality, and closing deals.
Difficulty is determined by cargo volume:
Modifiers:

rows: Destination has an INN (buyers gather there)
Caravan master has PATH OF TREASURE R2+
Caravan master has PATH OF WORDS R3+
Fellowship has local Standing +2 or higher
Cargo is Rare or Extremely Rare at destination
Market recently saturated (3+ caravans this season)
Fellowship has local Standing −1 or lower

segments.html: Results:

rows: Poor sale. Sell at ×0.75 of the calculated destination price. Buyers sense desperation or the goods do not match local need.
Fair sale. Sell at ×1.0 of the destination price. Standard market rate.
Good sale. Sell at ×1.25. The caravan master found the right buyer or timed the offer well.
Excellent sale. Sell at ×1.5. Premium buyer, bidding competition, or perfect timing. The buyer may also offer a standing order — guaranteed purchase of the same goods next season at ×1.25 rate.

segments.html: Standing orders guarantee a sale at a specific settlement for a specific cargo type at ×1.25 price, valid until the end of the next season. If the caravan does not deliver before then, the order lapses. Standing orders reduce sale risk but bind the caravan to a route. PATH OF THE CARAVAN R3+ characters can hold up to three standing orders simultaneously across different settlements.
If the caravan cannot sell all goods, the remainder can be:

• Stored at the destination (requires warehouse space — 1 silver per load unit per week, or free if the fellowship owns a stronghold with a WAREHOUSE).
  • Carried onward to the next destination, consuming load capacity and extending the journey.
  • Sold at loss (×0.5 price) to a bulk buyer or barter agent.
  • Donated for standing benefit (+1 Standing per 20 silver of goods).

• Carried onward to the next destination, consuming load capacity and extending the journey.
• Sold at loss (×0.5 price) to a bulk buyer or barter agent.
• Donated for standing benefit (+1 Standing per 20 silver of goods).

segments.html: When a caravan procedure roll in this chapter fails and the roll shows one or more ☠️, roll D66 on the table below.

• This applies to failed rolls such as loading, market sale, negotiation, field repairs, inspection handling, and similar caravan actions.
  • Resolve the normal failure result first. Then apply the mishap.
  • If several characters roll for separate caravan tasks in the same Quarter Day, only one roll with the most ☠️ can trigger a mishap.
  • No more than three mishaps per management week (excluding Hazards).

rows: Lose 3D6 silver of cargo value and one fragile load takes breakage check.
Accounting error. −1 on the next Market Roll this run.
As 2 ☠️ and the next contract payment is delayed one Quarter Day.
Lose 1 local Standing at this settlement.
Lose 1 local Standing and next ASK AROUND here is at −1.
Lose 2 local Standing; no standing order can be gained here this season.
Rival talk spreads. −1 on one negotiation at this stop.
Rival talk spreads. −1 on all negotiations at this stop.
As 2 ☠️ and one rival caravan result applies automatically next run.
One perishable load is unsellable (total loss).
Two perishable loads are unsellable (total loss).
Two dry-goods loads each lose 25% value.
Lose one Quarter Day and pay 1D6 silver in parts.
One draft animal cannot work for one day.
One draft animal cannot work for D3 days.
One draft animal is unusable until HEALING or ANIMAL HANDLING succeeds.
One hireling refuses risky duty for this day.
One hireling refuses duty until paid 1 day extra wage.
Two hirelings refuse duty; if unpaid they leave after one day.
Lose 2D6 silver and one named item from caravan gear.
Pay +1D6 silver or lose one Quarter Day rerouting.
Miss best market window. −1 on current Market Roll.
Miss market day entirely; sale delayed one Quarter Day.
Sale delayed one day and destination treated as saturated this week.
10% of sold value is delayed one week.
25% of sold value is delayed one week.
Dispute raised. Spend one Quarter Day proving terms or pay 1D6 silver.
Spend one Quarter Day and pay 1D6 silver in fees.
Spend one day and pay 2D6 silver; lose 1 Standing if unpaid.

Next two bandit-related hazard checks this run are at +1 frequency.

segments.html: If a result does not fit the current scene (for example, no animals in a river convoy), re-roll or adapt to the nearest equivalent cost in time, cargo value, or Standing.
At the end of a trade run, the caravan master calculates profit:

rows: Daily rate × number of employees × days traveled
1 copper/day per pack animal or draft animal (waived in grassland)
Per wagon or load unit at each TOLL HOUSE on the route
Crafting rolls and materials for vehicle damage
Cargo lost to breakage, spoilage, theft, or hazard
Loss. The caravan spent more than it earned. Common on first runs, long routes, or dangerous journeys.
Break-even. Covered costs but barely worth the time. Acceptable for route establishment.
Modest profit. A living wage for the peddler and crew. The standard for short, safe routes.
Good profit. Well-planned, well-executed. Enough to buy a second wagon.
Excellent profit. Rare — high-demand goods, low competition, or smart selling.
Windfall. Only possible with specialty goods at Extremely Rare prices, war demand, or market-beating information.

segments.html: Profit flows back into the system:
• More transport. Buy additional animals or wagons.

segments.html:
• Better escorts. Hire higher-tier fighters or a proper guard force.
  • Route expansion. Explore new markets and establish standing orders.
  • Stronghold investment. Fund MARKETPLACE, ROAD, BRIDGE, or WAREHOUSE functions.
  • Reputation spending. Buy reputation through feasts (10–20 silver), donations, or sponsorships.

segments.html: Each day of caravan travel, the GM rolls for hazards using the standard journey encounter rules (Chapter 8). When a hazard result occurs, roll D66 on the following table:

rows: Broken axle, washed ford, fallen tree. Lose one quarter day. CRAFTING roll to repair; failure adds another quarter day.
Perishable cargo damaged by weather or road conditions. Lose 1D6 silver per load unit of perishable goods.
Lame mule, bolting horse, ox refuses passage. Lose half a quarter day. ANIMAL HANDLING roll to resolve; failure means the animal is useless for a day.
Unexpected or inflated toll at a crossing. Pay 1D6 silver per wagon or MANIPULATION to negotiate. Failure means double toll or denied passage.
Rough terrain damages fragile cargo. Roll breakage check for all fragile load units.
Storm, fog, or downpour. Lose one quarter day. Open cargo takes water damage (1D6 silver loss per unsheltered load unit).
Pilferage at camp or during a stop. Lose 2D6 silver of goods unless a guard posted (SCOUTING roll to detect the thief).
Another caravan heads to the same destination with similar goods. When you arrive, the market roll takes a −1 modifier.
Riders watch the caravan from distance. Possible ambush ahead. SCOUTING roll to detect their number and position.
Armed attack. Use combat rules. Bandits target cargo first — breaking through the guard line, they cut loose 1D6 load units and flee.
Wolves, bears, or worse. Target livestock first, then work animals. ANIMAL HANDLING rolls to control draft animals during the attack.
A marked bridge is damaged or gone. Detour adds 1D6 quarter days, or CRAFTING roll to improvise a crossing (failure means cargo damage).
Disease strikes an employee or animal. Cannot work for 1D6 days. HEALING roll to shorten recovery.
Rockslide, fallen tree, flooded ford, frozen pass. Choose: detour (1D6 quarter days) or clear (1 quarter day + MIGHT roll; failure is 2 quarter days).
A warlord, bandit chief, or hostile settlement demands payment. 2D6 silver per wagon, or fight.
A settlement or patrol demands to inspect cargo. Legal goods pass; restricted goods (arms in some territories, contraband) may be confiscated or fined.
Wheel or harness breaks. CRAFTING roll to field-repair. Failure means the vehicle is immobile until proper repair (half day + materials).
A traveler, refugee, or stranded merchant on the road. They offer goods at bargain prices, intelligence about the route, or a delivery contract worth 1D6 × 5 silver at the next settlement.

segments.html: Hazard frequency. Larger caravans attract more attention: caravans of 4+ wagons add +1 to the

encounter die; 8+ wagons add +2. Guarded caravans deter some threats: caravans with 3+ visible guards reduce bandit-related results by re-rolling them as the next entry down the D66 table. Bandits prefer easier targets. Season matters: winter adds +1 to weather-related hazard frequency; summer reduces animal trouble frequency (−1 to those rolls).

The Forbidden Lands recognizes traders and caravans much as it recognizes settlers and hired blades. A fellowship that runs caravans regularly builds a name — the Caravan Circle, a reputation separate from Settlement Standing.
Caravan Circle Reputation is a single score (0–11+) tracking how well known the fellowship is among factors, innkeepers, toll-keepers, and other traders along the routes they travel.

rows: A few factors have heard the name.
Known along one or two routes. Established among local traders.
Reliable reputation across a region. Standing orders available.
Strong trade name. Premium access at major markets. Factors seek you out.
Major trader. Your caravan's arrival is news. Markets adjust.
Legendary trader. Settlements compete for your route.
Complete a trade run at profit
Fulfill a standing order on time
Deliver goods during crisis (famine, siege, plague)
+1 to +2 at that settlement and Chapter 8 Standing
Protect the route (clear bandits, repair bridges, mark roads)
+1 along the route (all settlements within 2 hexes)
Donate goods or fund MARKETPLACE or INN
Cheat, short-change, or deliver spoiled goods
Trade rumors from ASK AROUND gain +1 modifier when mentioning the caravan name.
Standing orders available without needing 3+ ⚔️ on the Market Roll. Factors and merchants approach with offers.
Buy price at regular origin settlements reduced 10% (volume discount). Sell price at regular destination settlements increased 10% (premium buyer trust).

Safe passage. Settlements along established routes maintain the road, warn of hazards, and refuse to harbor bandits who target the caravan. Equivalent to +1 Standing at every settlement within 2 hexes of the regular route.

segments.html: The Forbidden Lands economy shifts with the seasons. Demand, supply, risk, and profit all change. The caravan master who understands the cycle has an edge.

A season is the market interval, not the length of a single trade run. Resolve each caravan run in days and weeks: travel, sale, costs, and hazards. Apply seasonal multipliers by the current season at the point of sale. At each season boundary, refresh market conditions, rumor age, and contract windows.
One season is roughly three months (12 weeks), matching Chapter 9 cadence.
In winter, reduce expected runs by one bracket: travel takes longer and route risk rises.

rows: Recovery and planting. Rivers flood, roads thaw, villages reopen.
Grain demand peaks (spring hunger). River routes reopen. Road conditions poor — muddy, washed fords. Fresh goods commanded at premium prices.
Growth and movement. Roads dry, caravans move freely, markets active.
Best travel conditions. Competition highest — most caravans on the road. Prices normalize. Livestock trade peaks.
Harvest and preparation. Grain floods markets, villages stock for winter.
Grain prices lowest (harvest glut). Raw materials in high demand. Luxury goods spike (festivals, winter prep). Last safe window for long routes.
Contraction and scarcity. Snow closes passes, rivers freeze, villages shut down.

Travel costs +50%. Food and feed costs double. Many routes impassable. Prices spike at isolated settlements. Short routes between nearby settlements still viable. Bold traders profit most — if they survive.

segments.html: Apply these to the base sell price after the supply multiplier:

These stack with the supply multiplier. Grain that is Rare at a winter settlement sells at ×2.0 (supply) × ×2.0 (winter) = ×4.0 base price. That is how fortunes are made — and why bandits patrol the winter roads.
A caravan that sells its cargo at the destination faces a choice: return empty (sunk cost), buy return cargo (new investment), or find return work (paid for the journey home).

rows: Carry goods from destination back to origin or elsewhere
Anyone. More valuable for distant or dangerous routes.
Escort a person or small group along the route
Carry a specific item requiring careful handling

segments.html: Return contracts are found through ASK AROUND or SEEK WORK at the destination. Settlements with a MARKETPLACE or INN always have at least one return contract available. Smaller settlements may have none.
Passengers occupy one load unit of space. They bring their own food or pay 5 copper/day for meals. Passengers are non-combatants unless otherwise stated — they add mouths but not swords.
The PATH OF THE CARAVAN talent (Chapter 4) is designed for a world where caravans thrive. Here is how each rank interacts:

rows: Spend WP to deliver trade goods worth up to 1 silver/WP from ledger.
Suitable for personal-scale trade. No caravan assembly needed. The "ledger" is pre-purchased inventory.
Extend to weapons, 1D6 silver/WP per delivery. Establish a caravan cache.
The cache is a warehouse at a trading post. Costs 2D6 × 10 silver to establish (minus 2D6 per WP spent + a day of work). Holds up to 20 load units.
Each WP frees 2D6 silver of goods. Assign trusted factors. Passive income from absent trading legs.
Factors can manage a caravan without the PC. Uses the Market Roll at reduced skill (factor's MANIPULATION, typically 3 dice). Lose 1D6 silver per ☠️ per day absent.
Network covers heavy items, armor, shields, tools, raw materials.
Unlocks Arms and Armor and Raw Materials cargo at full value. Pre-R4 caravans carry them physically but cannot leverage talent discounts.
Masterwork designation or doubled purchasing power.
Masterwork goods sell at +50% (specialty tier). Doubled WP covers 4D6 silver per point, enabling high-value specialty trade without full cash investment.

segments.html: A character without PATH OF THE CARAVAN can still run a caravan. The talent is not a gate — it is a force multiplier. Without it: no ledger deliveries, no cache, no factor management (must be present for all trade), no arms or armor network, no masterwork trade. The un-talented trader makes money by smart selling and willingness to haul cargo personally.
Stronghold functions create lasting trade advantages. A fellowship that invests in infrastructure improves every future trade run on the affected routes.

rows: +1 to all Market Rolls at this stronghold. Attracts NPC caravans (passive income: 1D6 silver/week if staffed).
+1 to Market Rolls. Generates trade rumors. Attracts travelers and return contracts.
Reduces travel time on connected route by 1 quarter day per 2 hexes. Makes the route wagon-accessible.
Eliminates river-crossing hazards and delays on the route.
Required for barge loading/unloading. Opens river trade. Piers connected to other piers create high-speed trade lanes.
Generates passive income from NPC traffic (1D6 silver/week if the road sees regular use). Provides traffic intelligence.
Reduces animal upkeep costs by 50% at this stronghold. Provides replacement animals at standard price.
Stores up to 20 load units of trade cargo at no weekly cost. Cargo stored here does not spoil.

segments.html: Cost: 200 wood, 100 stone. One HOUSING consumed.

Effect: Stores up to 20 load units of trade cargo in a secure, dry space. Stored goods do not spoil. The warehouse is the physical anchor of PATH OF THE CARAVAN's cache — a proper one, not a field depot.
Upgrade — Large Warehouse: 400 wood, 200 stone. Two HOUSING consumed. Stores up to 50 load units.
A stronghold with MARKETPLACE and WAREHOUSE becomes a trade hub. NPC caravans seek it out. Passive income from the marketplace increases 50% (1D6+3 silver/week).
Use this procedure when caravan trade is background work rather than the center of play.
Pick a capital. The character commits silver to goods before leaving. This is the cargo cost.

Make a MANIPULATION roll when the run ends. Difficulty 1 for a small load (up to 5 load units). Difficulty 2 for a medium load (6–15 units). Difficulty 3 for a large run (16+ units). Apply the usual modifiers for MARKETPLACE, supply tier, and Standing.
Return on the roll:

rows: Loss. Recover 75% of cargo cost. The run went badly — spoilage, bad prices, or a hostile market.
Thin margin. Recover 110% of cargo cost. Wages and feed eat most of it.
Decent run. Recover 130% of cargo cost.
Good trade. Recover 150% of cargo cost.

segments.html: Subtract wages, feed, and tolls from the profit before counting gains. A drover and two guards on a two-week run cost roughly 15–20 silver in wages; fodder for three animals adds another 10–12 silver.
This resolves a trade run in a few minutes between sessions. Use the full system when caravan trade is central to play.
